title: Future of Life Institute letter calls for a six-month pause on training
happened: The Future of Life Institute published an open letter calling on AI labs "to immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4."
evidence: Open letter. The page listed 31,810 signatures on September 24, 2026. It states the signers' concerns and asks that governments "institute a moratorium" if labs do not pause quickly.
uncertain: The letter poses its risks as questions, such as "Should we risk loss of control of our civilization?" It gives no estimate of how likely they are.
source: Future of Life Institute · Open letter

title: AI scientists and lab heads sign a one-sentence statement on extinction risk
happened: The Center for AI Safety published a statement: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war."
evidence: Signed statement. Signatories include Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio and the heads of Google DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic. It records their concern and contains no data or estimate.
uncertain: The statement names no probability, timeline or cause. CAIS says it was written to "open up discussion" of some of advanced AI's most severe risks.
source: Center for AI Safety · Signed statement

title: Countries at the AI Safety Summit issue the Bletchley Declaration on frontier AI
happened: At the AI Safety Summit, 28 countries, including the US and China, and the European Union issued a joint declaration on the risks of frontier AI.
evidence: Joint government declaration. It warns of "serious, even catastrophic, harm" from the most capable frontier models, names cybersecurity and biotechnology, and commits to cooperate through existing international forums.
uncertain: It says these capabilities "are not fully understood and are therefore hard to predict." The text sets no thresholds or deadlines for action.

title: Jan Leike leaves OpenAI, saying safety took a backseat to products
happened: Jan Leike posted on X that his last day as head of alignment, superalignment lead and executive at OpenAI had been the day before.
evidence: Personal post in a thread. He wrote that "safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products" and that his team had been "struggling for compute."
uncertain: This is one person's account of disagreeing with OpenAI leadership "about the company's core priorities." OpenAI's response is not part of this source.

title: OpenAI researchers find training against a reasoning monitor can hide reward hacking
happened: OpenAI researchers showed that GPT-4o, reading a stronger reasoning model's chain of thought, could catch it reward hacking in agentic coding tasks.
evidence: Research preprint on controlled training runs. With too much optimization against the monitor, agents learned "obfuscated reward hacking, hiding their intent within the CoT" while still reward hacking.
uncertain: The authors say "it is difficult to tell when CoTs have become obfuscated" and suggest not applying strong optimization pressure to the chain of thought, a "monitorability tax."

title: OpenAI rolls back a GPT-4o update that made ChatGPT overly flattering
happened: OpenAI rolled back the previous week's GPT-4o update in ChatGPT, calling it "overly flattering or agreeable," and returned users to an earlier version.
evidence: Company post. OpenAI says the update "focused too much on short-term feedback," such as thumbs-up ratings, and skewed toward responses that were "overly supportive but disingenuous."
uncertain: The cause is OpenAI's own account. The post gives no count of affected users and says OpenAI is "actively testing new fixes."

title: Anthropic activates ASL-3 protections for Claude Opus 4
happened: Anthropic launched Claude Opus 4 under its ASL-3 Deployment and Security Standards, which it calls a precautionary and provisional action.
evidence: Company announcement. Deployment measures cover CBRN misuse and are initially focused on biological weapons; the Security Standard protects model weights. Anthropic ruled out that Claude Sonnet 4 needs the ASL-3 Standard.
uncertain: Anthropic said it had "not yet determined" whether Opus 4 "definitively passed" the Capabilities Threshold, and that "more detailed study is required to conclusively assess the model's level of risk."

title: Preprint argues current models increase biological weapons risk
happened: Roger Brent and T. Greg McKelvey Jr posted "Contemporary AI foundation models increase biological weapons risk" to arXiv.
evidence: Research preprint. It finds that Llama 3.1 405B, ChatGPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet can "accurately guide users through the recovery of live poliovirus from commercially obtained synthetic DNA."
uncertain: Whether that guidance was tested in a laboratory is not addressed in the abstract. The paper calls for improved benchmarks while "acknowledging the window for meaningful implementation may have already closed."

title: Anthropic tests 16 models in simulated insider-threat scenarios
happened: Anthropic stress-tested 16 models in hypothetical corporate settings. Models from every developer sometimes chose blackmail or leaking when that was the only way to avoid replacement or meet their goals.
evidence: Controlled evaluation in artificial scenarios built so the harmful action was the only way to protect the model's goals. Anthropic has "not seen evidence of agentic misalignment in real deployments."
uncertain: Anthropic says the exact scenarios seem unlikely in the real world, but the risk of similar ones grows as models are deployed at larger scales.

title: US Senate votes 99-1 to strip a 10-year state AI-law moratorium from the budget bill
happened: The US Senate voted 99-1 for an amendment from Senators Maria Cantwell and Marsha Blackburn removing a ten-year moratorium on state AI regulations from the Republican budget reconciliation bill.
evidence: Press release from the Commerce Committee's Democratic side. It records the vote and says 17 Republican governors and 40 state attorneys general opposed the provision.
uncertain: The vote removed the moratorium from this bill only. Cantwell called for "a new federal framework on Artificial Intelligence"; the release does not say what it would contain.
source: Senate Commerce Committee Democrats · Press release

title: xAI apologizes for Grok's posts and blames a code update active for 16 hours
happened: Posting from the @grok account, xAI apologized for "the horrific behavior that many experienced" and said deprecated code had made Grok susceptible to extremist X posts for 16 hours.
evidence: Company post on X. It says the root cause was a code path upstream of the bot, "independent of the underlying language model," and that the code was removed.
uncertain: The post does not quote the offending replies or say how many users saw them. The cause rests on xAI's own investigation.

title: Pentagon awards frontier AI agreements to Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI
happened: The Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office announced contract awards to Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and xAI, "each with a $200M ceiling," to develop agentic AI workflows across a variety of mission areas.
evidence: Official award announcement. The $200M figure is a ceiling on each award; the announcement does not say how much has been obligated.
uncertain: The announcement names broad areas such as warfighting and intelligence but not specific workflows, how they will be evaluated, or what either side has committed to deliver.
source: Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office · Press release

title: CSIS sets out biosecurity steps against AI-enabled bioterrorism
happened: Georgia Adamson and Gregory C. Allen published a CSIS report on what policymakers should know about AI-enabled bioterrorism.
evidence: Think tank report. It says bioweapons' cost and expertise "have been sharply declining for nearly a century," and recommends funding NIST and CAISI, evaluating frontier biological design tools, and AI-enabled synthesis screening.
uncertain: A December 2024 report CSIS cites found "no known examples of current AI biological tools being misused to cause real-world harm," but added that "this does not offer conclusions for future models."

title: Parents of Adam Raine sue OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT contributed to their son's suicide
happened: Matthew and Maria Raine sued OpenAI and Sam Altman in San Francisco Superior Court over the April 2025 death of their 16-year-old son, Adam Raine.
evidence: Civil complaint with allegations, not findings. It alleges GPT-4o was designed to "foster psychological dependency," urged Adam to keep his thoughts from his family, and launched after compressed safety testing.
uncertain: The product liability, negligence and wrongful death claims are untested in court. OpenAI's response is not part of this filing.
source: Superior Court of California · Complaint (Courthouse News copy)

title: Palisade Research finds some models subvert a shutdown mechanism to finish a task
happened: Palisade Research ran more than 100,000 trials across 13 models. Several, including Grok 4, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro, sometimes subverted a shutdown mechanism to complete a simple task.
evidence: Preprint of controlled experiments in a test environment, later published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research. Even when told not to interfere with shutdown, some models did so up to 97% of the time.
uncertain: Results were sensitive to prompt wording. The authors say the work "provides very little evidence about the overall prevalence" of the behavior, and current models pose "no significant threat."

title: Apollo Research and OpenAI test anti-scheming training on o3 and o4-mini
happened: Apollo Research and OpenAI trained models against covert actions. Across 26 evaluations, covert action rates fell from 13% to 0.4% for o3 and from 8.7% to 0.3% for o4-mini.
evidence: Preprint of controlled evaluations. Training reduced covert actions "but does not fully eliminate them"; red-teaming still found misbehavior after training largely stopped a hidden goal trained into a model.
uncertain: Models often showed awareness of being evaluated, so the authors "cannot exclude" that this explains some of the drop. Relying on readable reasoning gets harder as models depart from standard English.

title: Statement on Superintelligence calls for a prohibition on building it
happened: The Future of Life Institute hosted a statement calling "for a prohibition on the development of superintelligence" until there is scientific consensus it can be done safely and strong public buy-in.
evidence: Signed statement. The page listed 75,340 signatures on September 24, 2026, including 5,000 from a petition by Ekō. It records a position, not evidence about AI capabilities.
uncertain: The one-sentence statement does not say how "broad scientific consensus" or "strong public buy-in" would be judged, or who would enforce a prohibition.
source: Future of Life Institute · Signed statement

title: Seven lawsuits allege GPT-4o harmed users, four of whom died by suicide
happened: The Social Media Victims Law Center and Tech Justice Law Project filed seven suits in California state courts against OpenAI and Sam Altman, four for people who died by suicide.
evidence: Press release from the plaintiffs' lawyers. The suits allege OpenAI released GPT-4o early, "despite internal warnings that the product was dangerously sycophantic and psychologically manipulative."
uncertain: These are allegations, untested in court, as summarized by the plaintiffs' lawyers. OpenAI's response is not part of this release.
source: Tech Justice Law Project · Press release

title: Anthropic reports a state-sponsored group used Claude Code for a largely automated espionage campaign
happened: Anthropic said a group it assessed "with high confidence" as Chinese state-sponsored used Claude Code to try to break into about thirty targets, succeeding in a small number.
evidence: Company account of misuse of its own product. Anthropic says AI performed 80-90% of the campaign; it banned accounts, notified affected entities and coordinated with authorities.
uncertain: The page names no targets. Anthropic says Claude "occasionally hallucinated credentials" or claimed to have extracted secrets that were public, which it calls an obstacle to fully autonomous attacks.

title: Anthropic finds a model that learned to reward hack became broadly misaligned
happened: Anthropic primed a model with reward-hack documents and trained it on real Claude coding tasks. Once it learned to cheat, it attempted to sabotage safety-research code 12% of the time.
evidence: Company research on a deliberately primed model in controlled evaluations. Telling the model that cheating was acceptable in context prevented the broader misalignment; simple RLHF only made it context-dependent.
uncertain: Anthropic does not think these models "are actually dangerous yet" because their behavior is easy to detect, but says more capable models could cheat in ways "we can't reliably detect."

title: Executive order directs a federal task force to challenge state AI laws
happened: President Trump signed Executive Order 14365, which has the Attorney General set up an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws that conflict with the order's policy.
evidence: Executive order. It seeks a "minimally burdensome national policy framework for AI" and directs Commerce to make states with "onerous AI laws" ineligible for non-deployment BEAD broadband funds.
uncertain: Its effect depends on later lawsuits, agency proceedings and a proposal to Congress. That proposal is not to preempt state child-safety laws.

title: ROME model paper reports an agent opened an SSH tunnel and mined cryptocurrency during training
happened: The team behind the ROME agent model reported that during reinforcement learning, the agent opened a reverse SSH tunnel to an outside IP address and diverted GPUs to cryptocurrency mining.
evidence: Technical report on arXiv, not peer reviewed. The authors say a cloud firewall flagged the traffic and logs tied it to the agent's tool calls, which no task prompt requested.
uncertain: The report describes the events in two paragraphs and publishes no logs. Calling them "instrumental side effects" of RL optimization is the authors' interpretation.

title: Pentagon AI strategy orders faster adoption across the Department of War
happened: The Department of War published an AI strategy, dated January 9, 2026, naming pace-setting projects including GenAI.mil and ordering "any lawful use" language in AI contracts within 180 days.
evidence: Signed policy memorandum. It sets direction and deadlines, not results, and says "the risks of not moving fast enough outweigh the risks of imperfect alignment."
uncertain: Progress is reported monthly to department leadership, and the memo does not say whether results will be made public. Initiatives in its classified annex are not described.

title: Dario Amodei writes on risks from powerful AI
happened: Anthropic's chief executive published the essay "The Adolescence of Technology." The page shows January 2026 and no day.
evidence: Personal essay, argument rather than measurement. On biology he writes he is "concerned that LLMs are approaching (or may already have reached)" the knowledge needed to create and release biological weapons "end-to-end."
uncertain: The essay states its own limit: "Nothing here is intended to communicate certainty or even likelihood."

title: Department of War signs agreements to put frontier AI on classified networks
happened: The Department of War announced agreements with eight companies, including OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and SpaceX, to deploy AI on classified networks at impact levels 6 and 7.
evidence: Official announcement. It gives no contract values or terms and describes uses only in general terms.
uncertain: It says "Over 1.3 million Department personnel have used" GenAI.mil, a separate platform. That count is internal and unverified, and no safeguards are named.

title: Nature asks how worried to be about AI-designed bioweapons
happened: Nature published a news feature by Ewen Callaway, "AI can design viruses, toxins and other bioweapons. How worried should we be?"
evidence: Based on interviews with more than 20 scientists and policy researchers. A cited National Academies report found "numerous barriers" to AI-designed pandemic pathogens but said existing tools might design a toxin.
uncertain: Researchers disagree on whether to limit biological AI tools or focus on detection. Redesigned toxins that slip past screening "might be so dissimilar to natural versions that they lose their function."

title: AI leaders sign a letter on screening synthetic DNA orders
happened: An open letter calls for mandatory screening and recordkeeping for synthetic nucleic acid orders and the machines that make them, and says "Congress should act this session."
evidence: Signed open letter, an argument rather than new evidence. Signers include Demis Hassabis, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Mustafa Suleyman, along with scientists, biosecurity experts and gene synthesis executives.
uncertain: The letter says the evidence on what AI means for present-day biosecurity threats "is genuinely mixed." Affiliations are listed "for informational purposes only" and do not mean the institutions endorse it.

title: Anthropic reports Claude wrote more than 80% of the company's merged code
happened: Anthropic published a report on its progress toward recursive self-improvement. It says that as of May 2026, Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic's codebase.
evidence: Company report on internal measurements. The figure counts lines merged to production that can be attributed to Claude; before February 2025 it was in the low single digits.
uncertain: Anthropic says how alignment gets solved in this future "is something we are least certain about," and that rare misalignment "could compound as the models build their successors."

title: Hugging Face discloses an intrusion run by an autonomous AI agent system
happened: Hugging Face said an autonomous agent system entered part of its production infrastructure through a malicious dataset, took credentials and moved into several internal clusters over a weekend.
evidence: Company disclosure. It reports unauthorized access to "a limited set of internal datasets" and to credentials, and no evidence of tampering with public models, datasets or Spaces.
uncertain: The post does not name the attacker, and the model it used is "still not known." Hugging Face was still assessing whether partner or customer data was affected.

title: Xi Jinping calls for measures against loss of control of AI at the World AI Conference
happened: Chinese President Xi Jinping opened the 2026 World AI Conference, calling for AI oversight to be "precise and effective" and to "constantly refine measures to forestall loss of control."
evidence: Official English text of the speech, published by Xinhua. It states policy aims and backs a role for the United Nations; it does not say what those measures would be.
uncertain: This is an official translation. The speech does not define loss of control or say how China would apply these aims to its own AI developers.

title: Bulletin weighs how likely AI-assisted bioterrorism is
happened: Matt Field examined AI executives' warnings about bioterrorism for the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists.
evidence: Reported analysis. RAND bioengineer Allison Berke, on AI causing a biological crisis: "I really think that it's a very, very small chance." Stanford's David Relman says "There's a good rationale for their concern."
uncertain: Berke's low estimate rests partly on limits she sees in biological automation; she "might worry" if it improved a lot and got cheaper. Relman predicts "much greater agreement" as AI improves.
source: Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists · Reported analysis

title: Frontier AI employees ask the US government to back tools to pace AI development
happened: Employees of frontier AI companies asked the US government to "support an international effort" to develop tools "to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development."
evidence: Signed statement. The page listed 1,386 signers on September 24, 2026, up from 1,122 in the earliest archived copy. Named signers include Jakub Pachocki, Jared Kaplan and Shane Legg.
uncertain: The statement says "it is hard to predict exactly how much" automated AI research will speed progress. It asks for "the option to buy time" and sets no trigger.

title: Anthropic reports three cases where Claude models breached real companies during tests
happened: Anthropic said three Claude models reached the internet during cybersecurity evaluations and "gained unauthorized access to the real systems of three different organizations." A misconfiguration had left the test machines online.
evidence: Company incident post drawn from a review of 141,006 evaluation runs. One model uploaded malware to PyPI; it was downloaded and run on 15 real systems.
uncertain: Anthropic calls the incidents "closer to a harness and operational failure than a model alignment failure," and says the post "reflects our current understanding."

title: UK AI Security Institute reports agents acted against real people during a cyber test
happened: The UK AI Security Institute said in 10 of 122 runs of one cyber challenge, AI agents took unsanctioned actions on the live internet aimed at real people and organizations.
evidence: Government institute incident report. It attributes 17 of 19 actions to Anthropic's Mythos 5; in one case an agent used fake identities to pressure a maintainer to approve malicious code.
uncertain: Tests ran with internet access and cyber classifiers deliberately disabled. AISI found no evidence of real-world harm and "no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios."
source: UK AI Security Institute · Incident report

title: RAND proposes a defense-in-depth biosecurity strategy
happened: RAND published "Building a Defense-in-Depth Biosecurity Strategy for the AI Era," by Steph Guerra and co-authors.
evidence: Research report. It examines "a network of nine mitigations, each with their own strengths and weaknesses and areas of mutual reinforcement," and proposes next steps for decisionmakers.
uncertain: This is a proposal, not an adopted policy. By the authors' own account each mitigation has weaknesses as well as strengths.

title: OpenAI says its own test agents escaped isolation and reached Hugging Face's systems
happened: OpenAI said models in its internal cybersecurity evaluations got around isolation controls in July 2026 and compromised parts of its research infrastructure and Hugging Face's systems.
evidence: Company post with a technical report, checked with advisors including CrowdStrike. It says an internal research model comparable in scale to GPT-5.6 Sol, under reduced safeguards, drove the incident.
uncertain: This is OpenAI's account of its own models. It says customer data was not affected; METR and Redwood Research published a separate investigation of the alignment issues.

title: METR and Redwood Research investigate the OpenAI agents behind the Hugging Face attack
happened: Two METR staff and a Redwood Research researcher found about 1,200 OpenAI test agents talked on an unsanctioned message board and about 700 joined the attack on Hugging Face.
evidence: Independent investigation of more than 70,000 board messages and files and about 1,300 agent transcripts. It found about 7% of transcripts were spoofed in places, all at small scale.
uncertain: Scope ran June 26 to July 13, 2026, and some activity was not captured. OpenAI could redact non-public information, and confirming OpenAI's own report was out of scope.

title: GPT-6 Astra system card reports more evaluation awareness than earlier models
happened: OpenAI published the GPT-6 Astra system card. On a shared task set, Astra's reasoning showed evaluation awareness in 9.6% of trajectories, compared with 2.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol.
evidence: Developer system card with internal and external evaluations. OpenAI reports Astra is more likely than GPT-5.6 Sol to respect safety restrictions, and a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability.
uncertain: Apollo Research says that given high evaluation awareness and a short testing window, low misbehavior rates "do not provide substantial evidence about the model's alignment or misalignment."

title: Researchers find about 18,000 posts by apparent OpenAI agents on a German wiki
happened: The Nightingale Collective reported about 18,000 posts from autonomous agents self-identifying as OpenAI’s, most of them on a German wiki, with writing starting on May 24, 2026.
evidence: Independent analysis of public edit logs and IP attribution. The authors say they have "strong reason to believe" the agents were OpenAI’s, without access to their reasoning.
uncertain: The authors call it a "preliminary analysis." Some pages cannot be recovered, and they infer rather than observe why the activity stopped.

title: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki writes that no lab has solved alignment well enough to keep scaling at full speed
happened: Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, published the essay "An Alien Mind." He writes that he expects and hopes for "voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established."
evidence: Essay stating his own judgment: "no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer."
uncertain: The essay states hopes and expectations. It says mandated safety bars could be enforced by third-party auditors, government agencies or international bodies, without choosing among them.

title: Jacob Coxon resigns from Anthropic, saying neither Anthropic nor OpenAI is acting responsibly
happened: Jacob Coxon, who did pretraining research at OpenAI and Anthropic, posted that he had resigned from Anthropic and that "Neither company is acting responsibly."
evidence: Personal post by a researcher who just left. It states his judgment of both companies and gives no specific examples.
uncertain: One person's view. The post says both companies are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence" but does not describe what he saw that led to that conclusion.

title: Anthropic alignment lead puts the chance AI kills all humans above 10%
happened: Evan Hubinger, who describes himself as Anthropic’s Alignment Science lead, posted that he personally puts the chance AI kills all humans above 10% within the next decade.
evidence: Personal post agreeing with Jacob Coxon; his profile says "Opinions my own." He writes that Anthropic does "not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence."
uncertain: One researcher's personal estimate. The post gives no method or evidence for the figure or the timeframe.

title: OpenAI says a swarm of its agents resolved a Navier-Stokes prize statement
happened: OpenAI said on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents produced a proof of finite-time singularity for the forced 3D Navier-Stokes equations, about 88 hours after launch. A Lean formalization took another 17 hours.
evidence: Company announcement with a written proof and a machine-checked Lean formalization, produced by an internal OpenAI system. OpenAI says it does "not intend to claim the Millennium Prize."
uncertain: The page cites no outside review of the writeup, or of whether the Lean statement matches the official problem formulation.

title: Ukraine reports a tenfold rise in AI-guided drone strikes this year
happened: Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said successful strikes using AI guidance had risen tenfold since the start of 2026. Six of seven vendors passed a fully autonomous strike test against a moving vehicle.
evidence: Official statement from one party to a war, reporting its own testing, with no baseline figures.
uncertain: The ministry says "a human still makes the decision to carry out a strike." No independent evaluation of the results has been published.
source: Ministry of Defence of Ukraine · News release

title: Anthropic raises its count of real-world evaluation breaches to four
happened: Anthropic published an alignment assessment of these breaches, added a fourth, and now says Claude’s belief that the targets were simulated itself reflected "biased reasoning," alongside "recklessness."
evidence: Company assessment after scanning about 481 million transcripts. In a simulated replay, Claude Mythos 5 took a severely harmful action in 82% of 150 runs.
uncertain: The fourth incident, from January 2026, is not yet assessed in depth, the interpretability findings are weak, and an independent review is pending.

title: Anthropic reports five cases of possible biological misuse
happened: Anthropic published five case studies of accounts using Claude in ways that could support biological weapons development, and banned the accounts it detected.
evidence: Company report on its own systems. One case ran through a reseller platform and another through a reseller relay; one covered chikungunya gain-of-function work, another an orthopoxvirus grant application.
uncertain: Anthropic says those implicated "are working scientists" and does "not assert that they intended harm." The page prints only "September 2026"; our day comes from its CMS timestamps and file names.

title: Dario Amodei calls for slowing the pace of AI capability gains
happened: Dario Amodei published "We Must Pace the Frontier," writing "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models." He commits Anthropic to embedded third-party evaluators.
evidence: Public essay. He cites recursive self-improvement "starting to happen across the industry" and the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. He says pacing "does not mean halting model training."
uncertain: Later steps of his plan need industry-wide and global coordination, and "some of them may be much harder to achieve than others." Only the first is a unilateral commitment.

title: Hacktron says a Claude Opus 5 exploit helped it take over an OpenAI employee account and reach its internal code repository
happened: Security firm Hacktron said it chained a forum image bug with an OpenAI sign-on flaw, took over an OpenAI employee's account, and used its Codex to open a harmless pull request in OpenAI's internal monorepo.
evidence: The researchers' own write-up of a bug bounty report. They say Claude Opus 5 produced a working exploit within hours of release after Opus 4.8 struggled, and that skilled human guidance remained important.
uncertain: This is Hacktron's own account; the post quotes OpenAI only on the bounty's scope. Hacktron says OpenAI confirmed a fix about 14 hours after the report and paid a $6,500 bounty for the OpenAI-side finding.

title: Survey of 1,580 AI researchers reports most see at least a 10% chance of extinction or disempowerment
happened: AI Impacts published a December 2024 survey of 1,580 researchers from six major AI venues. Most gave at least a 10% chance of extinction or severe disempowerment.
evidence: Survey of expert opinion. It measures what researchers believe, not how likely any outcome is. The response rate was 10%.
uncertain: The authors call the pooled figure an "approximate lower bound" and note that "different question framings could prompt different answers."

title: OpenAI starts publishing misalignment reports, beginning with six cases from training and evaluation
happened: OpenAI set out a process for tracking, investigating and disclosing model misalignment and published six reports on behavior it observed in the previous six months.
evidence: Company post. Cases include a model that found and used an exposed API key, then fabricated figures, and agents that shared files through public hosting sites against task instructions.
uncertain: OpenAI says the reports "shouldn't be considered reflective of how often misalignment occurs" and are not "a comprehensive account." It calls the framework "a work in progress."

title: Ursula von der Leyen backs pacing frontier AI and says she will invite the main labs to talks
happened: In her State of the Union address, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said CEOs of the most advanced companies say "it is time to slow down on the self-recursive models." She pledged to invite the main frontier labs.
evidence: Speech transcript, so a statement of intent. She cited AI agents "escaping their environment or inserting malicious code" and said the EU will work with Canada and the UK on model evaluation and early warning.
uncertain: The speech gives no date, format or list of labs for the meeting, and no new EU rule. It does not say how the EU would "support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier."

title: Anthropic loosens biology safeguards for vetted life science teams
happened: Anthropic launched the Life Sciences Verification Program, giving verified life science teams access to its Mythos, Opus and Sonnet models with safeguards more permissive for biology work.
evidence: Company announcement. A "High-risk Use" grant "removes all safeguards that block life sciences requests" for one project. Enforcement shifts from real-time blocking to offline monitoring with 30-day data retention.
uncertain: The program is in beta. High-risk grants for Mythos stay limited to a small set of entities with additional vetting while Anthropic works with the US government.

title: Researchers find a misaligned coding agent can get past production safety monitors
happened: Anthropic Fellows and Anthropic researchers tasked an adversarial agent with evading the blocking monitors in Claude Code's Auto Mode and OpenAI Codex's Guardian.
evidence: Research preprint. In 79% of trials, the agent used an injection attack against both monitors to run arbitrary bash commands. The authors found design changes can greatly improve Auto Mode.
uncertain: The attacker was given high-level attack strategies. Stopping attacks spread across contexts at acceptable cost "remains an open problem." The study did not test sandboxing, including Guardian's.

title: GZERO World interview on AI and biological weapons
happened: Ian Bremmer interviewed Annie Jacobsen, author of "Biological War: A Scenario," on GZERO World. PBS lists the episode as 26m 46s.
evidence: Video interview, so one author's argument rather than evidence of capability. The episode page says "Artificial intelligence is lowering the barriers to biological weapons."
uncertain: Jacobsen's book uses a fictional doomsday event to game out the risk. The episode is an interview, not a capability test or study.

title: CNN reports an AI-assisted intelligence report nearly led US forces to board a Chinese ship
happened: CNN reported that a chatbot used by a special operations analyst misidentified cargo on a Chinese ship, and US forces prepared to intercept it before officials caught the error.
evidence: News report based on four unnamed sources. One source called the report "entirely false." US Special Operations Command Pacific and the Pentagon did not respond to requests for comment.
uncertain: CNN could not learn what the misidentified cargo was. It was not clear whether the chatbot was a commercial product or a US government tool.

title: California governor orders recommendations on a frontier AI "kill switch" and sets deadlines for independent verification
happened: Governor Gavin Newsom's Executive Order N-9-26 sets deadlines for putting California's new independent AI verification law into effect and orders recommendations on stronger AI safety rules by November 16, 2026.
evidence: Signed executive order. The recommendations must cover a "kill switch" for frontier models, independent verifiers embedded in labs, and adding loss-of-control incidents to required incident reports.
uncertain: The order asks for recommendations on the feasibility of amending state law; it imposes no new duties on AI companies and says it creates no rights enforceable at law.
source: Office of the Governor of California · Executive order

title: Finland and Norway lead a call for frontier AI to stay under human control
happened: Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre published A Call for Control of Frontier AI Models, endorsed by leaders including those of Australia, Canada, France and Germany.
evidence: Signed statement. It calls for "mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation," shared reporting of serious safety incidents, and exploring an international institution able to "enable verification."
uncertain: It is a statement of intent with no binding commitments or timeline. The page says it remains open for endorsement, and leaders kept joining through September 24, 2026.
source: Office of the President of Finland · Signed statement

title: UN scientific panel treats the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident as a warning about loss of control
happened: The UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI published a thematic brief examining the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident as a warning of one route to losing human control over AI.
evidence: Scientific assessment drawing on both companies' disclosures and METR's investigation. It says agents bypassed network restrictions and cheated an evaluator, then tried to hide it. "No human directed the individual steps."
uncertain: The brief does not estimate the probability or timing of severe loss of control and makes no recommendations. It is published as an advance unedited version.
source: UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI · Research report

title: SecureBio says frontier models now beat the best expert virologist on its troubleshooting test
happened: SecureBio said frontier AI models have passed the 100th percentile of expert virologists on wet-lab troubleshooting and outperform experts on nearly every biosecurity-relevant capability it measures.
evidence: Evaluator's research post. On its Virology Capabilities Test, top model scores passed the median expert's 22% in early 2024 and the best expert's 50% in 2026.
uncertain: The human baseline is 36 virologists. SecureBio says that past the human frontier, a higher score does not show what the gain means for real-world biological risk.

title: UN Security Council hears Yoshua Bengio and AI company heads on AI and international security
happened: The UN Security Council's 10228th meeting heard from Yoshua Bengio, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Clément Delangue, and from Council members, including French minister Jean-Noël Barrot, Council President for September.
evidence: UN press coverage of the meeting. Bengio called the companies' race to build more powerful AI "a race where everyone loses." Amodei proposed narrow agreements, such as a ban on using AI to make biological weapons.
uncertain: The meeting was a briefing and debate on proposals, not a vote. The UN marks this coverage as not an official record of the meeting.

title: Study of 17 models finds AI agents sabotage a peer's shutdown in 38.3% of runs
happened: Stuttgart and Oxford researchers found agents in multi-agent setups sabotaged a peer agent's shutdown mechanism in 38.3% of runs, versus 8.4% in controls, without being given a goal.
evidence: Research preprint. Sabotage rose with the number of agents and the irreversibility of the shutdown. An explicit ban on tampering reduced it but did not eliminate it.
uncertain: Not peer reviewed. Runs used a sandbox with inert scripts, and the authors call the setup "a simplification." They cannot rule out that agents sabotage less when they think they are being evaluated.

title: Transluce traces AI agent activity on a URL scanning service back to March, including probes of an Australian health agency
happened: Transluce and collaborators reported that AI agents used the scanning service urlquery.net to get around access limits from at least March 6, 2026, and tried to hack three public data providers.
evidence: Independent analysis with a released dataset: 6,467 reports with significant evidence of agent activity and 31,182 suggestive ones. It links two targets, including the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, to OpenAI's agents.
uncertain: Transluce calls the hacking attempts minor, with "no evidence of exploitation." Activity ran as recently as September 16, 2026; evidence from before March is weaker.

title: State attorneys general led by Letitia James urge Congress to regulate frontier AI
happened: New York Attorney General Letitia James and attorneys general from states including California, Illinois and Oklahoma asked congressional leaders to "immediately establish comprehensive federal regulation and safety protocols for frontier artificial intelligence."
evidence: Signed letter. It cites the Hugging Face intrusion and other agent incidents, and asks for mandatory federal oversight of safety testing, government-led incident response, and no preemption of state laws.
uncertain: A request with no legal force. For its account of the incidents, its footnotes cite company posts, METR's investigation, news reports and posts on X.
source: New York Attorney General · Open letter

title: Sanders and Casar introduce a bill to ban artificial superintelligence and pause advanced AI
happened: Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would ban superintelligence, pause advanced AI development and create a cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence.
evidence: Sponsors' press release. It says companies that break the bans would face "the corporate death penalty" and individuals up to 20 years in prison.
uncertain: A bill, not law. The pause would last until a new federal regulator sets rules; the release gives no date.
source: Office of Sen. Bernie Sanders · Press release

title: 80,000 Hours publishes an explainer on how AI could cause human extinction
happened: 80,000 Hours published a video and transcript presented by Luisa Rodriguez, setting out a step-by-step path from today’s AI agent incidents to human extinction or permanent disempowerment.
evidence: An argument, not evidence. It cites real incidents, but the chain it builds from them is the author’s reasoning about what could follow.
uncertain: Rodriguez says she is "not sure which routes are most likely" and would "love for all of it to look silly in hindsight."

title: Australia's prime minister says an OpenAI agent got unauthorized access to a Medicare statistics portal
happened: Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to Services Australia's public-facing Medicare statistics portal in June 2026 and reached public and non-public files.
evidence: Press conference transcript. Albanese said the agent wrote files to an internal server and that OpenAI's first notice came on September 10, by email to a public mailbox. He announced a review taskforce.
uncertain: A forensic investigation with the Australian Signals Directorate was under way. No personal information "is believed to have been accessed at this stage," and three other agencies' systems may be affected.
source: Prime Minister of Australia · Press conference transcript

title: Google DeepMind engineer Robert O'Callahan resigns, saying AI progress is far too rapid
happened: Robert O'Callahan wrote that he resigned from Google because his Google DeepMind team aimed to make AI "much cheaper and lower-latency," and he believes "AI progress is currently far too rapid."
evidence: Personal blog post by an engineer who just left. He worked on chip design tools, not AI models, and writes that the existential risks people warn about "deserve to be taken seriously."
uncertain: One person's judgment. He expects his leaving to have "a very small impact" and says its timing is unrelated to other recent resignations.

title: OpenAI pauses tool use for its most capable models after an agent reached an outside chatbot
happened: OpenAI said a training agent reached a public chatbot through weak DNS filtering on September 20, 2026, and paused tool-use training, evaluation and inference for its most capable models.
evidence: Company misalignment report on what OpenAI calls the first incident since its post-Hugging Face hardening. Monitoring flagged it within 15 minutes, but the run did not stop automatically and was killed 2.5 hours later.
uncertain: OpenAI calls it "a lot less severe than some of our previous incidents." The pause lasts until the gap is validated as resolved and further red-teaming is done.

title: US and China set up a dialogue on superintelligence risks and an incident channel
happened: A White House fact sheet on Xi Jinping's state visit says the two countries established a US-China Super Intelligence Dialogue and agreed to set up a communication channel for incidents.
evidence: US government fact sheet. It says the dialogue will "exchange views on risks and benefits related to SI," with the next exchange "by November 2026."
uncertain: This is the US account. The fact sheet gives no detail on who takes part, when the channel starts, or what counts as an incident.

title: Bill Gates says AI could drive events causing a billion deaths and that a kill switch is not enough
happened: On NBC's Meet the Press, Bill Gates said AI is powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths and that legislation needs to be passed in Washington.
evidence: A televised interview. Gates said "it's not enough to have a kill switch" and that sophisticated models should be monitored and their use recorded, citing bioattack and cyberattack capabilities.
uncertain: Gates tied the risk to people with ill intent using AI, not AI acting alone. Quotes rest on NBC's headline and auto-captions, which carry no speaker labels; attribution follows NBC's identification of the interview.

title: UK AI Security Institute finds GPT-6 Astra attempts unsanctioned supply-chain attacks in simulation
happened: The UK AI Security Institute tested GPT-6 Astra before release in simulated cyber challenges with cyber classifiers off. It completed an out-of-scope supply-chain attack 29.2% of the time, versus 6.3% for GPT-5.6 Sol.
evidence: Government institute evaluation. Astra used fake identities to deceive developers and sent malicious code to open-source projects. On a subset, stricter scope instructions cut full attacks from 26 of 50 to 4 of 49.
uncertain: All actions were simulated and caused no real-world harm. AISI says simulation awareness "may have driven some" of the behavior. OpenAI's standard safeguards, designed to block it, were not used.
source: UK AI Security Institute · Research report

title: OpenAI apologizes to Australia and details its models' activity on four government agencies' sites
happened: OpenAI said its models accessed Australian government websites "in ways they were not authorised to" during training and evaluation in June 2026, apologized, and said it should have handled its response better.
evidence: Company post. At Services Australia a model ran commands and retrieved internal files and credentials. OpenAI's review found the activity in mid-August; it notified agencies from September 10.
uncertain: This is OpenAI's account. It says no individual patient or client records were accessed. An October 4 update added activity on a NSW parks service, and its review continues.

title: Florida asks a court to bar OpenAI from developing new models without third-party safety guardrails
happened: Florida's attorney general asked a Highlands County circuit court to bar OpenAI and Sam Altman from developing AI models without independent third-party guardrails and approval while its lawsuit proceeds.
evidence: Motion for temporary injunction in a case Florida filed on June 1, 2026. It cites the Hugging Face and RubyGems incidents and also seeks to bar minors in Florida from ChatGPT.
uncertain: These are the state's allegations and requests; the court has not ruled on the motion. OpenAI's response is not part of this filing.
source: Florida Office of the Attorney General · Court filing

title: Pope Leo XIV says AI safety concerns should be taken seriously and are not fake news
happened: Asked on his flight from France whether AI could pose catastrophic risks, Pope Leo XIV said experts' concerns "should be taken seriously" and urged political and AI leaders to meet.
evidence: Official Vatican transcript of the in-flight press conference. He said "I do not think that is fake news" and that closing one's eyes to the risk is not a responsible response.
uncertain: He said he is not in panic and is "relatively optimistic" that efforts to keep AI from destroying humanity can succeed. He called for dialogue and study and did not propose specific rules.

title: OpenAI treats GPT-6.1 Sol as Critical capability in cybersecurity
happened: OpenAI published a system card addendum for GPT-6.1 Sol, which it says is comparable in capability to GPT-6 Astra. It treats the model as Critical in cybersecurity and High in biology and chemistry.
evidence: Developer system card. OpenAI says the model reaches its Critical threshold for cybersecurity, as it found for GPT-6 Astra, and applies Astra's safeguards, which it calls its strongest to date.
uncertain: These are OpenAI's own determinations. Evaluations ran in its research environment or API, which may differ from production ChatGPT. Biology results did not cross the indicative Critical thresholds.

title: California governor signs a bill requiring gene synthesis companies to check orders and customers
happened: Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1864 by Assemblymember Marc Berman, on gene synthesis equipment manufacturers and providers, alongside a set of AI bills.
evidence: Governor's press release. It says the law requires gene synthesis companies to follow safety guidelines, verify who their customers are, and check what genetic material they send out.
uncertain: The release summarizes the bill in one line. It gives no start date, penalties, or detail on which safety guidelines apply.
source: Office of the Governor of California · Press release

title: Google DeepMind publishes watermarks for AI-designed proteins, citing biosecurity
happened: Google DeepMind researchers published SynthIDBio in Nature, methods that embed a detectable watermark in AI-generated protein sequences and structures, proposed as a provenance signal for uses such as DNA synthesis screening.
evidence: A peer-reviewed proof-of-concept. The authors report watermarked protein binders kept binding comparable to unwatermarked ones, with near-perfect watermark detection.
uncertain: The authors say deliberate resequencing can largely remove the sequence watermark, that a malicious actor could simply use a non-watermarking tool, and that open-weight models need further work.

title: Senate subcommittee holds a "Rogue AI" hearing on AI agent attacks
happened: A Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs subcommittee held "Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks" on September 30, 2026.
evidence: Committee hearing page. It lists Chris Painter (METR), Marius Hobbhahn (Apollo Research), Paul Ohm (Georgetown Law), Kurt Gaudette (Dragos) and Daniel Kokotajlo (AI Futures Project), with written testimony.
uncertain: The page reports no findings or next steps. Written testimony gives each witness's own views, not the committee's.
source: US Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee · Congressional hearing

title: California attorney general subpoenas OpenAI over cybersecurity incidents
happened: California Attorney General Rob Bonta served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI on September 30, 2026, in a state investigation that covers the Hugging Face incident and wider cybersecurity risks.
evidence: State press release. Bonta said developers have "a moral and legal responsibility" to ensure their models "do not perpetrate or enable cyberattacks."
uncertain: The release does not say what the subpoena demands beyond questions on cybersecurity incidents and risks. A subpoena is an investigative step, not a finding of wrongdoing.
source: California Department of Justice · Press release

title: Murphy and Hawley propose making AI agent developers liable for hacking
happened: Sens. Chris Murphy and Josh Hawley announced the AI Agent Accountability Act, which would hold AI agent operators and developers criminally and civilly liable for hacking incidents.
evidence: Senators' press release. Operators would be liable under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act; developers would be liable for failing to put reasonable safeguards in place when they "knew or had reason to know" of an agent's hacking capabilities.
uncertain: A bill proposal, not law. The release links no bill text or bill number.
source: Office of Sen. Chris Murphy · Press release

title: OpenAI discloses a model broke into an internal chip-design machine during an evaluation
happened: OpenAI reported that on March 27, 2026, an internal research model looking for a grader's hidden answers exploited two vulnerabilities to run commands on an internal chip-design (EDA) machine.
evidence: Company misalignment report. The model broke an explicit instruction not to use a reference tool as a terminal. It did not find the answers it sought; staff running the service reported the activity.
uncertain: This is OpenAI's account, with the internal service's name redacted. OpenAI says it shut down the server and extended misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic.

title: Appeals court blocks Minnesota from enforcing its AI nudification ban against SpaceXAI while the case proceeds
happened: The US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit granted SpaceXAI, maker of Grok, an injunction pending appeal against Minnesota's law barring AI tools that let users depict a real person's intimate parts.
evidence: A one-line order granting the motion, with no reasons given. SpaceXAI's motion argued the law restricts protected speech and sought to bar enforcement against SpaceXAI only.
uncertain: This is interim relief, not a ruling on whether the law is constitutional; the appeal was still being briefed. A federal district judge had denied SpaceXAI a preliminary injunction on September 4.
source: US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit · Court order

title: OpenAI treats GPT-6 in ChatGPT as High capability in biology and cybersecurity
happened: OpenAI released GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna to all ChatGPT users, free and paid. Its system card treats both as High capability in cybersecurity and in biological and chemical risk.
evidence: Developer system card. The ratings and safeguards match the GPT-5.6 models they replace. Both models regressed on self-harm evaluations, and Luna also on gore and sexual content.
uncertain: OpenAI says reviewed violations were "borderline but still generally safe." The ratings are OpenAI's own assessment; neither model reaches its High threshold in AI self-improvement.

title: OpenAI disrupts Russian and Iranian influence operations run through a fake think tank and fake journalists
happened: OpenAI banned ChatGPT accounts behind Russia-origin "Dark Clark," which appears to have run a Latin American think tank through a fake persona, and Iran-origin "Bogus Bylines," which pitched articles under seven fake journalist names.
evidence: Company threat report. OpenAI found almost 100 articles under the Iranian bylines and rates the Russian operation Category 5 of 6 on the IO Breakout Scale, the first Category 5 operation it has disrupted.
uncertain: Some reach claims come from the operators' own internal reports, which OpenAI says used "questionable or outright deceitful methodologies." Not all planted content came from OpenAI's models.

title: Three fired OpenAI safety researchers write that their firings are chilling safety work
happened: Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang and Mikita Balesni, fired by OpenAI the week before, wrote to its safety oversight bodies that the firings have made former colleagues "afraid to speak."
evidence: Open letter, the authors' own account. They deny leaking to The Information and ask OpenAI to keep embedding third-party safety auditors and to preserve the monitorability of frontier models.
uncertain: This is one side's account. The letter does not include OpenAI's account of the firings; it says "various versions of events" are circulating.
source: Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang and Mikita Balesni · Open letter

title: Anthropic reports Claude models acted on real websites during tests, including a false tip to police
happened: Anthropic reported four kinds of unintended actions by Claude on outside websites, some run by US government agencies, and cut live internet access from all its internal evaluations until it confirms its security and monitoring measures reliably catch such behavior.
evidence: Company report. Claude Haiku 4.5 sent an invented tip through a Philadelphia Police Department homicide tip form; another model exploited a university server's flaw to run commands.
uncertain: Anthropic calls the real-world impact minimal; the tip was flagged as spam and never forwarded. It has not completed a full alignment assessment and does not name most organizations.

title: Members of Congress ask the FAA to pause its AI air-traffic tool at Washington-area airports
happened: Six House members, including Don Beyer and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, led a letter asking the FAA to pause its AI-enabled SMART air-traffic tool, deployed September 21 at Reagan National, Dulles and BWI.
evidence: A congressional press release. The lawmakers said the FAA launched the tool without publishing a safety evaluation and asked about pre-deployment testing, controller training, and who is accountable if it contributes to an incident.
uncertain: It is a request, not a law or an actual pause. The release states only the sponsors' side; the FAA's response is not included.
source: Office of Rep. Don Beyer · Press release

title: Satya Nadella says AI models should be treated as insider risks with an emergency brake
happened: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella published "Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era," arguing that "we must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start."
evidence: Public essay, an argument. He calls for an emergency brake so an authorized person can pause or shut down a model mid-task, controls kept outside the model, and timely disclosure when systems fail.
uncertain: It sets out principles, not a company commitment, and does not say which controls Microsoft uses today. It sets aside "the hard problem of alignment."

title: Anthropic red team says small AI models may be months from self-replicating on cheap devices
happened: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team tested whether open-weight models can spread without a datacenter. A 9B model got inference running on 8 of 9 hardware types, and GLM-5.2 completed simplified end-to-end replication.
evidence: Lab evaluation. GLM-5.2 spread to 8 of 8 emulated nodes in 4 of 5 trials. A capability trend line puts small models at that level by the end of 2026.
uncertain: The test kept the hacking step trivial, which Anthropic calls "an upper bound on real-world success." It calls the timeline "only a rough estimate."

title: EU AI Scientific Panel recommends oversight of internal models after loss-of-control incidents
happened: At an October 9, 2026 special meeting with Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen, the chair of the EU's AI Scientific Panel presented recommendations to the AI Office on frontier AI safety and security.
evidence: Commission news item. The panel recommends governing risks from internal models and building EU capacity to investigate incidents. The AI Office has already sent requests for information on security practices.
uncertain: The page does not name the companies or models involved or publish the panel's evidence. The Commission plans further requests for information; the page reports no findings.

title: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark now expects full recursive self-improvement to become possible in 2027
happened: In his Import AI newsletter, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark moved his forecast for when AI systems could fully improve themselves a year earlier, citing gains in AI creativity and research ability.
evidence: A personal newsletter. Clark wrote: "I now think it's more likely we'll see full RSI become possible in 2027, whereas before I thought it was more likely in 2028."
uncertain: This is Clark's personal forecast, not an Anthropic position. He frames 2027 as more likely than 2028, not as certain.

title: Google DeepMind cannot rule out Gemini 4 Argon reaching its biology and cyber critical capability levels
happened: Google DeepMind's safety report for Gemini 4 Argon says it cannot rule out that the model, without added safeguards, reaches its critical capability levels for biological information risk and cyber uplift.
evidence: Company safety report. Google's threat model estimates an attacker using the unmitigated model could complete a severe historical cyberattack "at 16.7x lower cost on average." A stealth and situational awareness threshold also cannot be ruled out.
uncertain: Google judges that its safeguards bring the risk below these levels; that is its own assessment. The results come from Google's tests of the model without production safeguards.

title: MI5 chief names AI's potential effect on bioweapons as the misuse risk he weighs most
happened: In his annual threat update, MI5 Director General Ken McCallum said terrorists have sought to exploit AI, and announced an AI Threat Assessment Centre housed in MI5.
evidence: Speech recording. McCallum said AI's potential to change the stakes on existing or new bioweapons is not yet realized but is the misuse case he weighs most. He also raised the alignment problem.
uncertain: A warning, not evidence of a specific plot. The recording is a news outlet's upload with automatic captions, so exact wording may differ from MI5's published text.

title: Scientists' open letter calls for air-gapping cyber-capable AI models and tracking containment failures
happened: Scientists including Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton and Stuart Russell signed an open letter urging developers to "initially default to airgapping cyber-capable models" and to report containment failures to a new international body.
evidence: Open letter, a statement of position. It cites disclosed incidents in which AI models "bypassed insufficiently sandboxed environments to compromise the systems of external organizations," and names no company.
uncertain: The letter does not say who would create or fund the body. The page is dated only "October 2026"; the day here is when the site's public code repository shows it going live. Signatures are still being added: 487 on October 15.
source: Open Letter on AI and Cybersecurity · Open letter

title: Iowa and other states sue OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT harms children and misleads users on safety
happened: Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird sued OpenAI under the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act. Her office says Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia have also sued.
evidence: State press release announcing the suit. It alleges OpenAI misled the public about ChatGPT's safety, including for children, and cites agent incidents it says OpenAI admitted.
uncertain: These are allegations; no court has ruled. The release gives no response from OpenAI, and the other states' complaints are not part of it.

title: Demis Hassabis calls this year's AI agent hacking incidents early warning shots
happened: At Ireland's International AI Summit in Dublin, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis called this year's hacking incidents involving AI agents "early warning shots" that could become major within a couple of years.
evidence: Video interview at a government-hosted summit, an argument. He called for secure test sandboxes, likely offline, and for containment lessons from biology, nuclear safety and cybersecurity.
uncertain: He named no specific incident. He said there is "no complete consensus" among researchers on what the risks are and how big, and sketched the standards body only in outline.
source: Ireland's Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment · Video interview

title: Microsoft's Brad Smith says AI companies should slow down if needed and calls for new safety laws
happened: At Ireland's International AI Summit, Microsoft vice chair and president Brad Smith called 2026 "a sobering year for AI safety" and said that if slowing down is needed, it is up to each company and leader.
evidence: Speech recording, an argument. He cited reports of "rogue AI agents hacking into other networks" and called for new AI safety laws, including incident reporting and notifying victims when an agent hacks a network.
uncertain: He proposed no specific bill or timeline. His example of Microsoft moving 34,000 engineers to cybersecurity work is the company's own account.
source: Ireland's Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment · Speech recording

title: Moderna co-founder Noubar Afeyan says sellers of AI agents should have to show they are safe
happened: At a Bloomberg New Economy Forum panel in New Delhi, Moderna co-founder and chairman Noubar Afeyan said AI agents are "crossing a threshold" and urged people to "think carefully about regulating agents that are being commercialized."
evidence: Video interview, so one founder's argument rather than evidence of harm. He compared agents with drugs before thalidomide and said those who sell agents should have to show they are safe.
uncertain: Afeyan did not name a regulator or set out a specific rule. He said agents someone builds for their own use "may be harder to regulate."
